nameStory: Hermaea cruciata gets its scientific name from the Latin 'cruciata' meaning 'cross-shaped' or 'marked with a cross,' likely referring to distinctive markings on its body. The genus name Hermaea comes from Greek mythology, named after Hermes, the messenger god known for his speed and ability to travel between worlds - fitting for a small sea slug that glides through underwater realms.
description: The cross-marked hermaea is a tiny sea slug that belongs to a special group called sacoglossans, which are shell-less marine snails that have adapted to life crawling along the ocean floor. These delicate creatures are among the smaller sea slugs you might encounter in New England waters. Like other sea slugs, they're soft-bodied mollusks that breathe through their skin and glide along surfaces using their muscular foot. With only one recorded observation in New England, this is truly a rare find for any tide pool explorer.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Small, elongated soft body that feels gelatinous and slippery to the touch, tapering toward the tail end

idTips.label: Cross markings
idTips.description: Look for distinctive cross-shaped or intersecting line patterns on the body surface - the key identifying feature that gives this species its name

idTips.label: Tentacles
idTips.description: Two small sensory tentacles (rhinophores) at the head end that may be retracted when disturbed

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly along surfaces using muscular contractions of its foot, leaving a slight slime trail

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Body surface appears smooth and translucent, feeling soft and slightly sticky when gently touched

habitat: Found in shallow marine waters along rocky coastlines and in tide pools throughout New England's coast. Look for them on algae-covered rocks, seaweed, or sandy areas near the low tide line where they feed. They prefer protected areas with good water circulation and abundant marine plant life.

seasonality.spring: Best time to spot them as waters warm and they become more active. Look during low tides when tide pools are accessible.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be seen gliding along algae-covered surfaces during low tide exploration.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may be less conspicuous as water temperatures begin to cool and daylight hours decrease.
seasonality.winter: Likely present but much less active in cold water; rarely observed during this season in New England waters.

funFact: Sacoglossan sea slugs like Hermaea are sometimes called 'solar-powered slugs' because many species can steal chloroplasts from the algae they eat and use them to photosynthesize their own food - essentially becoming part plant!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small sea slugs in tide pools, but the distinctive cross-shaped markings on the body are unique to this species. If you can't see clear cross patterns, you're probably looking at a different type of sea slug.
contextualKnowledge: Sea slugs are often mistakenly called 'sea snails,' but true sea snails have shells while sea slugs have evolved to live without them. The term 'sacoglossan' means 'sac tongue' and refers to their specialized feeding structure used to pierce algae cells.
compareHints: Since this is the only Hermaea species recorded in New England, compare it with other small hermaeidae family members by looking for the distinctive cross markings that set H. cruciata apart. Other hermaeidae sea slugs may have spots, stripes, or solid colors, but won't show the intersecting cross pattern that makes this species unique.
